One of the other two is the town where a man was kept dead a hundred years and then shown that his food had not spoiled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The man's final sentence is a correct confession offered at the point where it changes nothing about his garden, which raises the question the parable is built around: he could have said it any morning for years. The passage also identifies his fault precisely. He never worshipped an idol; he associated his own permanence with God's, which the Quran counts under the same name.

crossReferences.why: Completes the scene, noting he had no faction to help him and that authority belongs to God.
Uses the same phrase for a town fallen in on its supports, there as a lesson about revival.
Records a confession made as the water closes in, and the answer that it comes too late.

studies.applyIt: There is a sentence you would say if you lost something you currently have. Say it now, while you still have the thing. It costs nothing today and it is the entire difference between the two men in this parable, one of whom said it walking in and one of whom said it standing in the wreckage.

studies.title: There Authority Belongs To God
studies.meaning: The second thing he boasted of fails as completely as the first. He had no body of supporters to help him and could not help himself, which answers his earlier claim about manpower directly. The ayah then makes a general statement: in a moment like that, protection belongs to God, the True. Commentators read the same word in two ways, as protective friendship or as sovereign authority, and note that the sentence works under either reading.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city organised around clan protection. A man without backing had no legal standing, no redress and no safety, and the early believers who had been disowned knew this precisely. The parable's ending speaks to both sides of that arrangement at once: to those who relied on their faction and to those who had lost theirs.

keyTerms.note: A body of men who stand with you, used in the Quran for parties in battle. It names the practical form of protection in Arabia, which is why its absence here is a complete verdict.

From a root meaning nearness, giving both a protector who stands close and a ruler who holds power. Early readers vocalised the word two ways and the commentators accept both, since either sense fits.
From the root for a heel and for following behind. The word names what comes at the end of a sequence, so it grades the whole story rather than any single moment in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a formal thing, publicly declared and publicly withdrawn. A clan announced that a man was under its cover, and that announcement was what kept him alive on the road and solvent in the market. When cover was lifted, everyone knew within days. The parable's owner discovers the limit of an arrangement that ordinarily worked very well.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for protection in the second ayah was read with two different vowels by early reciters, giving either the friendship of a protector or the authority of a ruler. Both readings are preserved in the classical tradition, and commentators generally present them side by side rather than choosing, since the ayah supports each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say that human help is worthless. It says that at a certain point there is only one source of it, and it names that source with a word carrying both closeness and command. Reward and outcome are then both graded as God's, which closes the parable by moving from the man's ruined estate to a general statement about how anything ends.

crossReferences.why: Contains the boast about supporters that this ayah answers, word against word.
A man swallowed by the earth with no group to help him and no power to help himself.
States that God alone is the protecting friend, and that He gives life to the dead.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what you would turn to first if something serious went wrong: a person, a savings account, a professional contact. Do not cross anything off. Just look at the list and notice that you made it without effort, and that this ayah is describing the moment after every item on it has been tried.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Debris Scattered By The Wind
studies.meaning: A second parable follows immediately, and it compresses the first one into a single image. Water comes down, plants take it up and mingle with it, and then the whole growth becomes dry fragments that the wind carries off. The commentators note the speed of the sentence, which moves from rain to debris without a pause. The closing clause names God as having complete power over everything, which is what makes both the growth and the scattering His.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just shown a wealthy man losing an estate, and this parable generalises that case so it is not read as one unlucky owner. Rain in Arabia was sudden, brief and transformative, so the audience did not need the comparison explained. They had watched a valley turn green and then turn brown inside a few weeks.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal verb for two things becoming intertwined. The plants do not simply receive the water; they mix with it, which is why their drying is a separation as much as a death.
Vegetation broken into brittle fragments, occurring only here in the Quran. The word names the texture rather than the state, so it describes what the growth feels like in the hand once it is over.
To winnow, the verb for tossing threshed grain into the air so chaff blows away. Applying it here makes the wind a sorter, not just a destroyer, which fits a passage about what remains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Winnowing was ordinary work. After threshing, grain was thrown up in the air on a breezy afternoon so the heavy seed fell back and the light husk blew off. Every farming household did it and every listener had watched it. The parable uses that familiar action to describe the whole of worldly life, with the sorting already built into the picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to set out a parable for them appears three times in the Quran, and two of those occurrences are in this surah, opening the story of the two gardens and opening this one. The two parables are placed thirteen ayat apart and the second is a fifth the length of the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison is not to death but to a cycle in which growth and dispersal belong to the same process. Nothing in the image is wasted or wrong; the plants did what plants do. What is corrected is only the expectation of permanence. Naming God's complete power at the end keeps the passage from reading as a lament about time, since the sequence is described as governed rather than merely observed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same comparison at greater length, adding the moment people think they have mastered the land.
Sets the same image inside a list of what worldly life consists of, ending in withered debris.
Follows immediately, naming what lasts once the wind has carried the rest away.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that filled your attention completely five years ago and that you have not thought about in months. Not a loss, just a thing that mattered enormously and then dispersed. Naming one is enough. The parable is not asking you to care less today; it is asking you to notice that this has already happened, repeatedly, without your permission.

studies.title: The Things That Last
studies.meaning: Two things are named and neither is condemned. Wealth and children are called the ornament of this life, which grants that their attraction is real and located exactly where the surah placed it earlier. Set against them is a phrase left deliberately open: the lasting good things. The commentators offer a range for what it covers, from remembrance and prayer to any righteous act, and most decline to narrow it. The comparison is made twice, in reward and in hope.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows the parable of the man with two gardens who told his companion he had more wealth and a stronger following, and whose gardens were destroyed overnight. It also follows the image of the world as vegetation that rain raises and wind scatters. The commentators report no specific occasion. Placing the ayah there makes it the conclusion of a story rather than a general maxim.

keyTerms.note: An active participle of remaining, in the feminine plural, with no noun attached. The absence is what makes the phrase famous: it names a category and leaves the reader to fill it.
From a root meaning to come back. The reward is described as something returning to the one who sent it out, which is a different picture from a prize handed over at the end.
The word for what a person leans forward towards. Saying the lasting things are better as hope means they are the better thing to want, which is a claim about the present rather than the future.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth and sons were the two measures of a man in that society, and they were connected. Sons meant hands for the herd, riders in a feud, and someone to keep your name. A rich man with no sons was pitied; a poor man with many was still counted. Naming exactly those two as ornament was naming the whole scoring system the audience used on each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the lasting good things appears twice in the Quran, here and in another Meccan surah, both times in the same phrase and both times in a comparison. Reports from the companions attach it to particular phrases of remembrance, while many commentators keep it wide. Both readings have circulated side by side since the earliest period.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does not ask anyone to stop valuing wealth or children. It ranks them, which is a different operation, and it ranks them by duration rather than by worth. That leaves ordinary attachments intact while removing their claim to be ultimate. The second comparison is the sharper one. Saying the lasting things are better as hope reaches into what a person spends the day wanting, which is harder to adjust than what they spend it doing.

crossReferences.why: The other occurrence of the same phrase, closing on return rather than on hope.
The parable this ayah concludes, about a man whose two gardens made him certain.
Lists the same attractions in more detail and calls them the enjoyment of this life.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you hoped for when you woke up this morning. Not what you believe you should hope for: the actual first thought. Write it down in five words. Then leave the note somewhere you will see it in a week. This ayah compares two hopes rather than two possessions, and the comparison only works if you know what yours is.

studies.title: The Earth Laid Bare
studies.meaning: Three things happen in one sentence. The mountains are set moving, the earth appears stripped and level, and everyone is gathered with no one left out. The commentators read the middle clause as the removal of everything that stood on the surface, so the ground is shown without its features. The final clause is the one that carries the weight: not a single person is passed over, which turns a cosmic scene into a personal one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the last day in the early revelations are short, physical and delivered without argument, addressed to people who found the idea of universal gathering implausible. This ayah arrives just after two parables about things that looked permanent, so the dissolution of mountains reads as the same lesson at maximum scale.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something travel, used of caravans and of clouds. Applied to mountains it does not say they are destroyed, only that the least movable thing in the landscape is made to go somewhere.
Something that has come out into the open with nothing in front of it. Occurring only here in this form, it presents the earth as exposed rather than damaged, a surface with no cover left.
A verb for leaving something out, related to the word for treachery, since to abandon a person is to break faith. Used in the negative it says the gathering has no omissions and no exceptions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed reference of Arabian life. Travellers navigated by peaks, tribal territories were described by them, and a mountain on the horizon was how you knew where you were. Nothing in the visible world was more permanent. A description of them being made to move would have registered as the removal of the last thing anyone could steer by.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb saying that no one will be left out appears only once in the Quran, and its root is the same one behind the Arabic word for treachery, the breaking of a trust. The choice quietly frames being overlooked at the gathering as a betrayal that will not occur.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a specific anxiety about universal judgement, which is that individuals get lost in a large number. Its final clause denies exactly that. It also completes a movement running through the surah, where things assumed to be stable are shown to be held in place rather than fixed by nature: sleepers, gardens, harvests and now mountains.

crossReferences.why: Describes the mountains scattered as dust and the earth left as a level plain with no crookedness.
Lists the folding of the sun and the moving of the mountains among the signs of that day.
The parable just before, where the same lesson about impermanence is drawn from a season of rain.

studies.applyIt: Look at the largest fixed thing you can see from where you are, a building, a hill, a road. Hold it for a moment as something that has a duration rather than as background. This ayah is not asking for dread. It is asking you to move one item from the category of permanent to the category of long, which is a change you can actually make.

studies.title: As We Created You First
studies.meaning: They are brought forward in ranks, and the first thing said to them is about their condition: you have come exactly as We first made you. The commentators read this as arriving without possessions, without status and without the arrangements that made one person outrank another. The sentence that follows names what they had claimed, that no appointment would ever be set. The reply does not argue the point. The gathering itself has already settled it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The denial of any final meeting was a fixed position among the city's leadership, and the surah has just shown a wealthy man holding it inside a garden. This ayah moves the same claim to the moment it is tested, and it does so directly after the parable, so the two read as one continuous argument.

keyTerms.note: A line of people standing level with one another, used of prayer lines and of battle formations. The image removes the arrangement of seats and precedence that ordered every gathering the audience knew.
A verb the Quran reserves for assertions made without warrant. It carries a faint contempt in Arabic usage, marking a statement that was confidently repeated and never supported.

A fixed appointment in place and time, from the root for promising. The word appears four times in this surah alone, twice in these few ayat, binding the destroyed towns and the gathered people to the same arrangement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public assemblies in Mecca were ordered by rank. Where a man stood in a gathering, who spoke first, who was seated and who remained on his feet were all read instantly by everyone present, and the arrangement was the visible form of a clan's standing. A description of the whole of humanity in a single level row would have struck that audience as a specific dismantling.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for an appointed meeting occurs four times in this surah, and two of those are in consecutive scenes here: the appointment people denied would ever be set, and the appointment fixed for the destruction of the towns. The same term covers a person's final summons and a civilisation's expiry date.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies what is stripped away rather than what is added. Nothing new is imposed on anyone; everything acquired since birth is simply absent, which makes the original creation the measure. The denial is then quoted back rather than refuted, because the setting has become the argument. Being present at the meeting you said would never happen leaves nothing for either side to say.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing at greater length: you have come to Us alone, leaving behind what We granted you.
Continues the scene, placing the record in front of them and finding everything already counted.
Describes someone coming to God alone, stripped of the wealth and children he had spoken of.

studies.applyIt: Take off the things you are wearing that signal something, a watch, a badge, a title in an email signature, and just notice how much of your sense of yourself is attached to them. You do not have to change anything. The ayah is describing an arrival where none of it comes with you, and getting familiar with that is not a morbid exercise.

studies.title: It Leaves Nothing Uncounted
studies.meaning: The record is set down and the reaction is immediate. What alarms them is not severity but completeness: a book that omits nothing small and nothing large. The commentators note that they do not dispute a single entry. They find what they did present in front of them, and the ayah closes with a clause that anticipates the objection nobody raises: your Lord wrongs no one. The accuracy is what makes the fairness possible.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience for whom writing was the specialised skill of a few and a written record was an instrument of trade and treaty rather than of daily life. Describing judgement as the opening of a ledger drew on something they trusted precisely because it was rare and formal, not because it was familiar.

keyTerms.note: A word for fear mixed with care, the state of someone anxious about an outcome they are invested in. It is not terror, which is why it fits people reading rather than people fleeing.
From the root for pebbles, which were used for tallying. The verb means reckoning by discrete units, so nothing is summarised or estimated; each item was set down as one.
Not remembered or reported but physically at hand. The word turns the past deed into something in the room, which is a stronger claim than any description of a record could make.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Merchants in Mecca kept accounts, and a caravan's investors settled up on return against written tallies that were read aloud in front of witnesses. Anyone who had ever been on the wrong side of that reading knew the particular silence of a column of figures being gone through item by item, and the impossibility of arguing with a number that had been recorded at the time.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb saying the book leaves nothing out is the same one used two ayat earlier to say no one will be left out of the gathering, and it occurs only twice in the Quran. Both times it is negated, so the Book uses the word only to deny that anything or anyone gets missed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is grounded here in information rather than in severity. A complete record makes both wrongful conviction and quiet escape impossible, and the closing clause states that no one is wronged as a consequence of the accuracy, not as a concession alongside it. The passage also treats deeds as durable objects rather than as vanished events, which changes what an action is.

crossReferences.why: The ayah just before, with the same verb used to say no one is left out of the gathering.
States the same completeness in the smallest possible unit, an atom's weight of good or evil.
Places a record around each person's neck and tells them to read it themselves.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things you did yesterday that nobody saw and nobody will ever mention. Not the good ones especially, just three. The point is not guilt. It is to feel, briefly and concretely, what it means for small unwitnessed things to be the kind of thing that gets written down at all.

studies.title: He Was Of The Jinn
studies.meaning: The scene of the command to bow is recalled in a single clause, and then the ayah supplies a detail found nowhere else: he was of the jinn, and he broke out of his Lord's command. The Quran then turns on the listener with a question. Will you take him and his descendants as protectors instead of Me, when they are your enemy. The parable of the two gardens has just shown what a bad exchange looks like, and the final word here is the word for a swap.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabian religion involved dealings with unseen beings: travellers sought protection from the jinn of a valley before camping, and diviners claimed access to them. The question here addresses a real practice rather than an abstract error, and the surah has already established the theme of choosing the wrong partner and losing everything.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a date breaking out of its skin. The image is of something departing the covering that held it, so disobedience is pictured as stepping outside a boundary rather than as an act of hatred.

Those you turn to for support and who have a claim on your loyalty. The word is about practical reliance, which is why the question is phrased as a choice between two protections rather than two opinions.
What you receive in place of something given up. The word grades the transaction, and the ayah calls it wretched, which is the language of a trade gone badly rather than of a crime.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of the unseen was practical and everyday. A man entering an unfamiliar valley at night would call on its master among the jinn for safe passage, and the custom was widespread enough that the Quran addresses it directly elsewhere. Illness, madness and sudden misfortune were commonly attributed to them, and there were people in every district who claimed to deal with them.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names this figure eleven times, and this is the only ayah that says what he was. Every other passage places him among the angels being addressed or describes what he did, and the single clause here is the entire textual basis for a question the commentators discussed at length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds a warning about alliance in a piece of history: the being now solicited for protection is the one who refused the command at the beginning. It also frames misplaced trust as a transaction rather than a mistake, which raises the question of what was given up. And it names enmity as a fact about the relationship, not a feeling on either side.

crossReferences.why: Describes men seeking refuge with individuals among the jinn, and only increasing them in burden.
Gives the same scene with the refusal argued out, and the reason offered for it.
States that this enemy is an enemy, and tells people to treat him accordingly.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you actually turn to first when something frightens you at two in the morning. Not what you would say you rely on, but what your hand reaches for. This ayah frames protection as a choice you have already made without deciding it. Name yours honestly this week, without judging it yet.

studies.title: I Did Not Call Them To Witness
studies.meaning: The argument is made by denial. Those being taken as allies were not present at the making of the heavens and the earth, and they were not present at their own making either. The second clause is the sharper one. Then a general statement closes it: God does not take those who mislead as a support. The commentators read the word for support as literally the upper arm, so the claim is that nothing has ever been leaned on in the running of the world.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's religion assumed intermediaries with standing before God who could be approached on a worshipper's behalf. This ayah does not attack the intermediaries' character; it asks about their credentials, which is the same move the young men in the cave made earlier in the surah when they asked for clear authority.

keyTerms.note: To have someone present at an event so their testimony counts afterwards. Witnessing in Arabia established a legal claim, so the denial removes any standing they might have had to speak about creation.
An active form: not merely lost themselves but taking others off the path. The word describes a role rather than a state, which is why it can be set against the idea of being a helper.
The word for the arm between shoulder and elbow, used for the person you lean on. Occurring only here in the Quran, it makes the denial physical rather than abstract.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the backbone of Arabian dispute. A claim about a boundary, a debt or a marriage stood or fell on whether men had been called to witness at the time, and the phrase for summoning witnesses was ordinary legal language. Using it about the creation of the world places the whole question in a courtroom the audience knew how to sit in.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for support in this ayah is the ordinary Arabic term for the upper arm, and it occurs only once in the entire Quran. Related forms of the same root appear elsewhere for strengthening someone, so the metaphor of an arm that others lean on was live rather than dead in the language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine independence is argued from the record rather than asserted. If no one was present, no one has a claim, and the argument is available to any listener without special knowledge. The second clause is quietly devastating: those being asked to intervene in the world were not consulted about their own existence. The passage grounds a doctrine in a fact anyone can check about themselves.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the angels were created female while the speakers were witnessing, the same challenge about presence.
Describes gods who create nothing and are themselves created, and hold no power over harm or benefit.
The youths in the cave make the same demand of their people, asking what authority stands behind their gods.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you defer to without examining it, an expert, a tradition, an instinct you inherited. Ask the question this ayah asks: what was it actually present for. Not to discard it, but because deferring to something you have never located the credentials of is exactly the habit being described.

studies.title: Call On My Partners Now
studies.meaning: The instruction is given as an experiment. Call the ones you claimed shared in My authority. They call, and nothing answers. The Quran does not report a refusal or an excuse; there is simply no reply. Then something is placed between the two parties, and the word for it is used nowhere else in the Book. The commentators read it as a place of destruction, a barrier, or a valley that separates, and they record the range without settling it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The whole social value of the Kaaba's associated deities lay in access: a worshipper expected an answer, a rain, an outcome. The surah keeps returning to the moment when an arrangement is tested, in the ruined garden and again here, and each time the test is simply whether the thing relied on responds.

keyTerms.note: To call to someone at a distance, the verb for shouting across a valley. It presumes separation and hope of being heard, which is precisely the assumption the scene is testing.
An assertion made without evidence, appearing three times in this surah. The Quran uses it consistently for a confident position that was never examined by the person holding it.
From a root for perishing, occurring only here in the Quran. Commentators read it as a barrier, a pit, or a valley of destruction set between them, and preserve the alternatives rather than choosing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling across distance was a real skill. Herders signalled between hillsides, caravans kept contact by shouting between sections of the line, and a call unanswered on open ground meant something had gone wrong. The scene here uses that physical experience: voices going out over a space, and the specific quiet that comes back when there is nobody there.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for what is placed between them appears only once in the Quran, and the classical commentators offer at least three readings of it: a barrier, a pit of destruction, or a valley of flowing fire. Rather than deciding, the major commentaries list the possibilities, which is how they usually handle a term with a single occurrence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage tests a relationship rather than refuting a belief. Nothing is said about whether the partners exist; what is shown is that they do not answer. That shifts the criterion of a real object of worship to responsiveness, which is a standard the Quran applies elsewhere too. The separation placed between them afterwards makes the failure permanent rather than momentary.

crossReferences.why: Says that if you call them they do not hear, and if they heard they could not answer you.
Gives the contrasting case: God is near, and answers the call of the one who calls.
Describes calling on those who cannot answer until the Day, and are unaware of being called at all.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you actually expect to answer when you are in trouble: a person's message, a search result, a bank balance. Then notice how you feel in the gap before it responds. That gap is the subject of this ayah. Spend one of those gaps this week saying something to God instead of refreshing the screen.

studies.title: Most Argumentative Of All
studies.meaning: The sinners see the fire and understand where they are going, with no way to turn aside. Then the passage steps back and comments on itself. Every kind of comparison has been set out in this Quran for people, and the human being is the most argumentative of things. The commentators read the second ayah as the explanation of the first: the material was supplied and varied, and the response to it was not incomprehension but dispute.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at a point in the surah where four parables and two narratives have already been given. The self-referential comment lands with weight because the reader has just been through them. The classical commentators connect it to the Meccan pattern of answering each new argument with a fresh objection rather than an assessment.

keyTerms.note: A place to be diverted to, occurring only here in the Quran. The root behind it means turning something away, and it appears again in the very next ayah for varying a message.

keyTerms.gloss: We have varied, We turned about
keyTerms.note: To turn something this way and that so it can be seen from every side. The same word is used of shifting the winds, so the message is described as presented in changing forms rather than repeated.
From a root for twisting rope strands tightly together. Arabic uses it for argument that grips and will not release, so the noun describes tenacity rather than intelligence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dispute was a prestige skill. Tribes kept orators who could argue lineage, honour and grievance in public, and a man who could hold a point against pressure was admired for it. Poets were paid to win exchanges. Naming argumentativeness as the human being's most characteristic quality would have landed in Mecca as an observation about their finest talent.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat share a root. The word for a way to turn aside, which the sinners cannot find, and the word for the varied presentation of the Quran come from the same three letters. One means being diverted and the other means turning something about so it can be examined, and they sit in consecutive sentences.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the failure of communication on the receiving side without denying that the material was adequate. Every kind of comparison was supplied, so the shortfall is not in clarity. It also makes an anthropological claim rather than a moral one: argument is what human beings are most inclined to do, which is stated as an observation before any blame is attached to it.

crossReferences.why: Says the same message has been varied in this Quran so they may remember, and it only increases aversion.
Notes that only those who disbelieve dispute about the signs of God, and warns against being impressed.
Continues the point two ayat later, describing argument used deliberately to unseat the truth.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement, try to name what would actually change your mind, before you say anything else. If you cannot name it, you are doing the thing this ayah describes. It takes about thirty seconds and it usually changes the conversation more than any point you were about to make.

studies.title: Nothing Prevented Them But This
studies.meaning: The question is asked and then answered by an exception that is really an accusation. What stopped people from believing and seeking forgiveness once guidance reached them, except that they were waiting for the pattern of earlier peoples to come round to them, or for punishment to arrive in front of their faces. The commentators note the structure: no obstacle is named, because there was none. What is described instead is a wait, and what is being waited for is the last thing anyone would want.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's leadership had reportedly challenged the message to produce the destruction it warned about, which is the demand this ayah answers. The surah has already listed the towns that were destroyed. Presenting the challenge as a form of waiting rather than of courage reframes a taunt the audience would have recognised as their own.

keyTerms.note: A way of doing things that has been laid down and repeats. The Quran uses it for the regularity in how communities that reject warning come to an end, so it names a precedent rather than a threat.
Placed alongside believing as a second thing they were prevented from. The pairing matters: what is being described is not only an intellectual refusal but the absence of a turn back.
Directly before them, in plain view. Early readers vocalised the word two ways, giving either punishment confronting them openly or punishment in successive kinds, and both readings are preserved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The ruins of earlier peoples were not abstractions in Arabia. The rock-cut facades in the north lay on the trade route to Syria, and caravans from Mecca passed them. Traders knew the stories attached to those sites and repeated them. Referring to the pattern of the ancients pointed at buildings the audience had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the punishment coming upon them was read with two different vowel patterns by early reciters, yielding either punishment arriving face to face or punishment arriving in successive varieties. Both readings are recorded in the classical literature, and commentators generally set them side by side without preferring one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies that unbelief has an intellectual cause in this case. No argument is named, no confusion, no missing evidence. What is named is a posture of waiting for confirmation of a specific kind, which by its nature arrives too late to be useful. Seeking forgiveness is placed next to believing, which suggests the barrier is as much about admitting fault as about accepting a claim.

crossReferences.why: Records the demand that stones rain from the sky if this really is the truth from God.
States that you will find no alteration and no turning in God's established pattern.
Names the towns destroyed for their wrongdoing, with an appointed time set for it.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you are waiting for before you change something you already know needs changing. Write the answer in one sentence. Most people find that the thing they are waiting for is a consequence, which means the plan is to be forced. Knowing that about yourself is not a small piece of information.

studies.title: Only Bearers Of News
studies.meaning: The messengers' role is stated in two words and nothing else: bringing good news and giving warning. The commentators note what the definition excludes. There is no mention of compelling, of governing hearts, or of producing results. Then the opposing activity is described with equal precision: arguing by means of what is empty in order to make the truth slip. The final clause names the tone, taking the signs and the warnings as a joke.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, during the years when the message was met with mockery more often than with force. The classical sources record specific taunts and nicknames used in the city. This ayah does not answer them; it defines the messenger's job in a way that makes the taunts irrelevant to whether he is doing it.

keyTerms.note: From the word for skin, since news shows first in the face. The verb means to deliver something that visibly changes a person's expression, which is a more physical idea than announcing.
The opposite of truth, but its root sense is a thing that is void, useless, come to nothing. Arguing by it is not arguing dishonestly so much as arguing with material that has no substance.

keyTerms.gloss: so as to make it slip
keyTerms.note: From a root for a slippery place where a foot loses grip. The image is of trying to make the truth lose its footing rather than of defeating it in open argument.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with a technique. Satirical poets were commissioned to ridicule rivals, their verses were memorised and repeated at markets, and a well-made insult could damage a family's standing for a generation. Mecca's response to the early message drew on that established practice, which is why the Quran addresses ridicule so often and so specifically.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for making the truth slip comes from the root for slippery ground, and the Quran uses the same root for the ground a garden becomes after it is ruined earlier in this surah. Argument that unseats and land that will not hold a foot are described with the same word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The definition limits the messenger's responsibility to delivery, which protects both him and his hearers: he is not answerable for their response, and they are not being managed. The passage also describes bad argument accurately, as an attempt to destabilise rather than to refute. That distinction is useful, because the two look identical from inside a conversation and differ entirely in aim.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit directly: you are a reminder, you are not in control over them.
Notes that messengers before were mocked, and what they ridiculed closed in on the mockers.
The ayat just before, where human argumentativeness is named as the response to every kind of parable.

studies.applyIt: If you carry religion into conversations, try separating what you are responsible for from what you are not. You can say the thing clearly and warmly. You cannot make it land. Pick one relationship where you have been quietly measuring your success by their response, and set that measure down for a month.

studies.title: Coverings Over Their Hearts
studies.meaning: Two acts are described before any consequence: he was reminded of his Lord's signs and turned away, and he forgot what his own hands had sent ahead. Only then does the ayah speak of coverings over hearts and weight in ears. The commentators are careful about the order, reading the sealing as following the turning rather than preceding it. The closing clause states the result plainly, and it is the bleakest sentence in the surah.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to men who had heard the message repeatedly over years and had settled into a fixed response. The same imagery of covered hearts and heavy ears appears in three other places in the Quran, always about audiences who had been given ample exposure rather than about people encountering the message for the first time.

keyTerms.note: Cases or sheaths that enclose something to keep it hidden, from the root behind the word for a nest. The image is of protective covering, so the heart is shielded from what it does not want.
A weight, and by extension a dullness of hearing. The word for a heavy load shares the root, so the ear is described as carrying something rather than as broken.
To send something on ahead of you, as goods are sent ahead of a traveller. Deeds are pictured as already dispatched to the destination, waiting, which is why forgetting them is possible and useless.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Goods were sent ahead of a caravan to a destination where an agent received them, and a merchant arriving would find his own consignment waiting. Nobody would forget what he had sent. The metaphor here would have struck a Meccan trader as absurd in exactly the intended way: a man who has dispatched a shipment and cannot remember what was in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of coverings on hearts paired with heaviness in the ears occurs four times in the Quran, in almost identical wording. In every case it follows a description of people who had already heard the message and turned from it, which is the sequence the classical commentators rely on when they read these ayat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage raises the hardest question in the Quran about guidance, and it answers it by sequence rather than by argument. The turning away is described first and attributed to the person; the covering is described second and attributed to God. Commentators broadly read this as a consequence set in motion by a choice, which preserves both the divine act and the human responsibility that the ayah opens with.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image of veiled hearts and heavy ears, of people who turn away when God alone is mentioned.
Describes a sealing of hearts and hearing, following a description of settled refusal.
Says rust has covered their hearts because of what they were earning, naming the cause directly.

studies.applyIt: Think of a criticism you have heard more than twice from different people and dismissed each time. Do not act on it yet. Just write it down accurately, in their words rather than yours. The condition this ayah describes begins with turning away, and the smallest available counter-move is writing something down instead of moving past it.

studies.title: He Would Have Hastened It
studies.meaning: After the bleakest ayah in the surah, the tone turns. Your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy, and the reasoning that follows is a conditional: if He were to take them to task for what they have earned, He would have hurried the punishment. He has not, so the delay itself is being read as evidence of mercy. But an appointment stands, and the towns already destroyed are cited to show that the appointment is real and that it has a time attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience had demanded the promised punishment and taken its non-arrival as proof that the warning was empty. These ayat interpret the same delay in the opposite direction. The ruined settlements referred to lay along routes Meccan traders used, so the second ayah points at evidence the listeners had seen with their own eyes.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root meaning to cover over, related to the word for a helmet. Forgiveness in this word is protection placed over a fault rather than a fault declared not to have happened.
The ordinary verb for acquiring by work or trade. Applying it to deeds makes wrongdoing something accumulated deliberately, like a balance, rather than something that merely happened to a person.
A place you retreat to for safety, occurring only here in the Quran. The root means to return or resort somewhere, so the denial is that there is anywhere left to go back to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Arabia ran on deferred settlement. A merchant extended terms, a date was fixed, and everyone understood that patience before the date was not cancellation. A creditor who did not collect immediately was showing forbearance, not weakness, and everyone in the market knew the difference. The audience heard this ayah with that distinction already available to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a refuge in the first of these two ayat occurs only once in the Quran. The word for an appointed meeting occurs in both ayat, binding them together: the people have an appointment they cannot escape, and the destroyed towns had one set for their destruction. The same term does both jobs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delay is reinterpreted as an attribute in action rather than as absence or indifference. The conditional sentence makes the point precisely: the punishment did not arrive, and the reason given is not that it was undeserved but that God is forgiving. At the same time the passage refuses to let mercy dissolve the appointment, which keeps forbearance from becoming a guarantee.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same argument at greater scale: if God took people to task, no creature would be left on earth.
States that He defers them to an appointed term, and when it comes they cannot delay or advance it.
Notes how many towns were given respite while wrongdoing, and then seized.

studies.applyIt: Consider a consequence you have been spared, at work, in a friendship, in your health. Not one you avoided by skill, one that simply did not arrive. Sit with the possibility that the delay was a gift rather than a verdict of innocence, and use one hour of it today for something you have been putting off.

studies.title: Until I Reach The Junction
studies.meaning: A new story begins with no introduction and no explanation of why the journey is being made. Moses tells his young companion that he will not stop until he reaches the meeting place of the two seas, or travels for an age. The commentators note the resolve in the phrasing and the vagueness of the destination. He knows there is a meeting point and that someone is there; he does not know where it is, and the ayah does not tell the reader either.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the third of the surah's four narratives, and it follows immediately on ayat about people who will not learn. The classical commentators identify this Moses with the prophet of the Torah, on the strength of a well-known report, and record that an early alternative suggestion was raised and rejected. His companion is generally named in those reports as Joshua.

keyTerms.note: The singular of the word used earlier in this surah for the youths of the cave. It covers a young man who serves and travels with someone, carrying attendance and youth together rather than servitude.
A verb meaning to leave a place, negated to mean continuing without stopping. The construction expresses persistence by denying departure, so the resolve is phrased as a refusal to turn back.
A very long period, which classical lexicographers put at many decades. Occurring only here in the Quran, it sets the outer limit of a search someone is genuinely prepared to keep making.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Long journeys in Arabia were undertaken with a companion and without maps. You travelled toward a described landmark, asked at each stop, and adjusted. The phrase for the meeting of two waters would have sounded like an ordinary navigational description to the audience, the kind of destination a guide gives when the precise spot is known only when you arrive.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a long age used at the end of this ayah occurs only once in the Quran. So does the phrase for the junction of the two seas, in the following ayat. The whole episode is built from vocabulary that appears nowhere else, which is one reason its geography has never been settled by the commentators.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet is shown setting out to learn something, which establishes that receiving revelation does not exhaust what a person can be taught. The passage also models a search with an unknown endpoint and a stated willingness to spend an unlimited time on it, which is a description of how seeking knowledge actually works rather than an idealisation of it.

crossReferences.why: Names what the journey was for: a servant given mercy and taught knowledge from God's own presence.
Contains the instruction to ask for an increase in knowledge, the only such request in the Quran.
Continues the journey, with the forgotten fish and the request for lunch that marks the turning point.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you have decided you already understand well enough. Then find one person who knows it better than you and ask them a real question about it this month. The journey in this story is undertaken by someone who had every reason to think he had been told what he needed.

studies.title: They Forgot Their Fish
studies.meaning: They reach the junction and forget the fish, which takes its way into the water and slips off. Then they travel past the place, and hunger arrives before the realisation does. Moses asks for lunch and says the journey has worn them out. The commentators note that the fish was the sign, and that they walked away from the meeting point because nobody was watching for it. The exhaustion that makes him ask for food is what sends them back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's third narrative unfolds in short scenes with almost no explanation, a style the classical commentators contrast with the fuller stories of Moses elsewhere in the Quran. Nothing in the text names the location of the junction, and the identifications offered in the commentary literature are presented as reports rather than as established geography.

keyTerms.note: A dual verb, so the forgetting is shared. Arabic marks two people distinctly from a group, and the form quietly spreads the lapse across both of them rather than blaming the servant.
A burrow or channel, occurring only here in the Quran. The word makes the fish's route through the water sound like a hole left behind it, which is how the commentators describe the scene.
Physical exhaustion from effort. Its appearance here is the first hint that something has changed, since the commentators note that the tiredness only began after they passed the meeting point.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dried or salted fish was standard travelling food. It kept without spoiling, weighed little and needed no preparation, which made it the ordinary provision for a journey on foot along a coast. Carrying one and losing it was an unremarkable mishap. The story sets its turning point on the smallest possible domestic detail.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the fish's route into the water occurs only once in the Quran, as does the word for the junction of the two seas and the word for a long age in the previous ayah. Three consecutive ayat each contain a term used nowhere else in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sign is missed at the moment it happens and recognised only afterwards, which is how the passage describes almost all recognition. Fatigue, the most ordinary of complaints, is what turns them around. The narrative suggests that the appointed meeting was never in danger of being lost, since the very thing that looks like failure is what brings them back to the right place.

crossReferences.why: The servant explains what happened to the fish, and Moses recognises it as the sign they were seeking.
Sets out the destination and the resolve, which this ayah shows them reaching without noticing.
Another moment where those present do not perceive the significance of what is happening to them.

studies.applyIt: Look back at one week that felt like wasted effort and check whether something started there that you only noticed later. Not to manufacture meaning. Just to practise the specific attention this story is about, which is looking back at the point where you were tired and had stopped paying attention.

studies.title: The Sign They Walked Past
studies.meaning: The young companion answers the request for food with a confession. Back at the rock, the fish was gone, and he had forgotten to say so; he blames the devil for the lapse and adds that the creature took its way into the water astonishingly. Moses does not scold him. He says this is precisely what they were after, and the two turn round and follow their own footprints back. The commentators note that the sign is recognised only once the failure is reported.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the third of the surah's four narratives. The classical commentators read the whole episode as a lesson given to Moses about the limits of what any servant of God is granted to know, and they connect it to the surah's larger argument against people certain their own knowledge is complete. Nothing in the passage names the rock or the shore, and the sources treat the geography as report rather than record.

keyTerms.note: The definite article makes it a particular rock the two of them already know, though the text never says which one. The word names a single large mass of stone rather than stony ground.
One word carries a subject, a causative verb, an object and a person: something made me forget it. Arabic compresses into a few letters and two suffixes what English needs a whole clause to say.
The same word appeared in the surah's opening question about the sleepers in the cave. Its two uses here attach to a company held for centuries and to a fish slipping into water.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers on a long walk carried dried or salted fish, bread and water, and stopped at a landmark to sit out the worst of the heat. A boulder big enough to throw shade was a fixed point on a route, remembered and named. Younger companions carried the provisions, and losing the day's food on a coastal road was a real problem rather than a detail. They had already passed their meeting place before hunger raised it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for astonishing that closes this ayah occurs four times in the Quran, two of them in this surah. The other is in the opening question about the people of the cave. Once it describes a company of sleepers held for generations, and once a fish taking its way into the sea. The surah does not rank the two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A journey undertaken at God's direction proceeds by way of a forgotten errand and a servant's apology. The sign is not withheld and then granted. It is given, missed, and recovered by walking back. That is a claim about how guidance actually reaches people who are looking for it: inside ordinary lapses rather than around them, and here it took admitting the lapse out loud to find it.

crossReferences.why: Earlier in this surah, forgetting is met with an instruction to remember God, which is what this scene stages.
Adam is described as forgetting a covenant, and the lapse is stated plainly rather than excused or condemned.
Names the same cause of forgetting and says what to do once the memory comes back.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you noticed today and did not mention. The boy's report is late and it is still what turns the journey around. If something you should have said is sitting with you now, say it to the person who needs it, plainly, without dressing it up as anything other than a thing you forgot.

studies.title: A Servant Given Knowledge
studies.meaning: They find a servant, and the ayah describes him entirely by what he was given: mercy from God's presence, and knowledge from God's own side. He is not named, and no lineage, town or office is supplied. The commentators identify him from a well-known report and then differ over whether he was a prophet or a righteous man granted particular knowledge, recording the disagreement rather than settling it. What the text itself supplies is the source of what he knows.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reports describe the surah as answering questions put to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by his opponents, questions about a sleeping company, a traveller who reached the ends of the earth, and the spirit. This episode sits among them and answers none of the three. The commentary literature treats the servant's identity as a matter of report, and the reports vary in their detail.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, and left indefinite. The Quran names dozens of figures and withholds this one's name, so every description of him has to run through what he was given rather than who he was.

A word of immediate presence, closer than the ordinary word for from. It marks the knowledge as handed over directly rather than acquired, and a standing term for divinely given knowledge was later drawn from it.
Placed before knowledge, and introduced by a different phrase: mercy from Our presence, knowledge from Our side. The order puts the gift of compassion ahead of the gift of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge in that world moved by apprenticeship. A boy learned poetry by sitting with a poet, tracking by walking behind a tracker, trade by carrying goods for an uncle. You attached yourself to someone and travelled with him, and what you learned came in the order he chose to give it. Moses is about to ask for exactly that arrangement, and the refusal he gets is about the arrangement rather than about him.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered from Our own side occurs six times in the Quran, and this is the only place where what follows it is knowledge. Elsewhere it introduces a great reward, tenderness, a remembrance, provision, and an amusement God says He would decline to take. The word marks a gift as arriving straight from God rather than through any intermediate cause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates a kind of knowing that no method reaches. Moses is a prophet given a scripture, and he is sent to learn from someone whose knowledge came by an entirely different route. That the servant goes unnamed keeps the point from turning into a biography. What is established is that God distributes understanding unevenly and deliberately, and that being given much does not mean being given all of it.

crossReferences.why: A prophet is taught to ask for an increase in knowledge, which is the request Moses is about to make.
The angels answer that they know nothing except what God taught them, the same limit stated from the other side.
States as a principle what this meeting stages: above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.

studies.applyIt: Pick someone who knows something you do not and ask them to teach you a piece of it this week. Say what you want to learn and let them set the order. The hard part is not the asking; it is accepting a sequence you did not design, from someone who is not obliged to explain why they began where they did.

studies.title: May I Follow You
studies.meaning: Moses asks permission rather than assuming it, and asks for a portion rather than the whole: some of the sound judgement you were taught. The answer is not a refusal but a prediction, and then a reason. How is anyone to endure what he has not encompassed in knowledge. The commentators treat that second sentence as the key one. Impatience here is not being named as a flaw in Moses. It is the predictable result of watching without understanding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, within the third narrative of a surah built from four stories about people tested by what they hold or lack. The classical sources place this meeting after Moses had already been sent, which is what gives the request its weight: a prophet carrying a revealed law asks a stranger for instruction. The commentators discuss the sequence at length and report no specific occasion for these particular ayat.

keyTerms.note: Not information but the maturity to act well on it. The word occurs twice in the Quran, here and in a passage about orphans judged ready to be handed their own property.
From a root meaning to surround like a wall. Knowledge that encompasses leaves no gap on any side, and the question is whether Moses has that kind of hold on what he is about to see.
Knowledge from the inside, of the sort a man has of his own valley. It occurs twice in the Quran and both times in this surah, the second in the narrative that follows this one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guides were hired for desert crossings, and the whole arrangement rested on not arguing. A guide who turned off a straight-looking track, or refused a well, was reading signs the traveller could not: a wind pattern, a raiding party's range, water gone bitter. Caravans that overruled their guides died. The condition being set here would have sounded entirely ordinary to anyone who had crossed sand behind someone else.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Moses uses for what he hopes to be taught occurs only twice in the whole Quran. Its other appearance is in an instruction about orphans, where it names the sound judgement that shows a young person is ready to receive his own property. This narrative ends with two orphans waiting to reach exactly that threshold.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet who has spoken with God asks to be taught, and is told he is not equipped for it. The passage separates rank from comprehension. Being chosen does not make a person's understanding complete, and the gap is stated without embarrassment. It also gives a reason for impatience that is not a moral one: people cannot bear what they cannot see the shape of, which ties patience to knowledge rather than opposing them.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for sound judgement, there as the sign that an orphan is ready for his own property.
States the principle the coming scenes will dramatise: your reading of an event is made with less than the facts.
Lists what no human being knows, marking the boundary the servant's warning draws around Moses.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you form a firm opinion about a situation you have only watched from outside. Before you say it, name one thing you would need to know to be sure. You do not have to withhold the judgement. Just carry the missing piece alongside it for the rest of the day and see whether it changes shape.

studies.title: You Will Find Me Patient
studies.meaning: Moses promises patience and attaches a condition to it in the same breath: if God wills. The commentators treat that qualification as the sentence's real content, since he is undertaking something he has just been told he cannot deliver. Then he adds obedience to endurance. The reply sets one term, and the term is about speech rather than conduct: ask me nothing until I bring it up myself. What is forbidden is questions, not watching.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A few ayat earlier in this surah, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is instructed never to say he will do a thing tomorrow without adding that God wills it, an instruction the classical sources connect to a pause in revelation after a question had been put to him. Moses says exactly that here, which the commentators note as the narrative practising what the surah had just taught.

keyTerms.note: An active participle, naming a state he expects to be in rather than an act he will perform. The root covers restraint, endurance and confinement, and its underlying image is tying a thing down so it cannot bolt.
From a root meaning for something to come into being. The servant does not promise explanations. He reserves the right to originate the subject, so any understanding will arrive as a new event.
The same root as remembrance, and the word the Quran uses of itself. What is withheld from Moses is not the deed, which he will watch happen, but the account of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise carried weight close to legal weight, and a man who bound himself to a companion for a journey had made something like a contract. Adding a condition was ordinary prudence, because the desert broke plans as a matter of routine: a well dry, a tribe hostile, a camel gone lame. Saying you would do a thing without qualification was heard as a claim about a future nobody owned.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where Moses says the phrase for if God wills. The expression occurs six times in all, spoken by an Israelite crowd, by Joseph, by Abraham's son at the moment of sacrifice, by the man of Midian, and once in a promise about entering the sacred mosque. Here it belongs to Moses alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A commitment is made and immediately handed back. The passage lets a prophet promise something and mark the promise as not entirely his to keep, which is what makes the later failure something other than a broken word. It also shows patience being defined by its object. Moses is not asked to tolerate discomfort. He is asked to hold silence in the presence of things that look wrong, which is a harder and narrower discipline.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction Moses is following here, a few ayat before this narrative begins.
Abraham's son answers a far harder request with the same conditional phrase and the same promise of patience.
The man of Midian is told he will be found among the righteous, again with the condition attached.

studies.applyIt: Take one commitment you have made for tomorrow and say it out loud with the condition attached: if God wills. Then notice what changes in how you hold it. The point is not to weaken the promise or leave yourself an exit. It is to say a true sentence about a day you have not been given yet.

studies.title: He Tore The Boat Open
studies.meaning: The condition lasts exactly as long as the first act. They board, the hull is holed, and Moses speaks. His objection is precise: he names the deed, states its apparent purpose, and delivers a verdict on it. Nothing in the passage suggests his reading of what he saw is inaccurate. What he lacks is not observation but the reason behind it, and the word he reaches for to condemn the act is used nowhere else in the Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the first of three acts the surah tells in the same shape: a journey resumed, an inexplicable deed, an outburst, a rebuke. The classical commentators read the repetition as deliberate structure rather than narrative padding, and note that the three move from damaged property to a death and then to unrewarded labour, so the objection changes character each time it is raised.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of rending or piercing a surface: cloth torn through, a hull breached. This form occurs once in the Quran, and the objection that follows immediately throws it back as a question.
A word used only here in the Quran. The commentators gloss it as something monstrous or disastrous, and observe that it names the sheer size of the act rather than sorting it into a moral category.
Definite, although no vessel has been introduced. Arabic uses the article for a thing made present by the scene itself, so the boat simply appears at the moment the two of them step into it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's coasts ran a small-boat economy. Fishermen and short-haul carriers worked the Red Sea and the Gulf in wooden hulls stitched with palm fibre and sealed with fat or pitch. A boat was a family's entire capital, patched constantly and handed down. A hole below the waterline was not vandalism in the abstract. It was the difference between a household that ate that month and one that did not.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Moses uses to condemn the deed occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, and the verb describing the holing of the boat appears in this form only here as well. The scene is told in vocabulary that never recurs, while the rebuke answering it repeats, word for word, a clause the servant had already spoken before the journey started.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A correct description of an event can still be a wrong account of it. Moses reports accurately and judges wrongly, and the gap between the two is filled by information he does not have and will be given later. That is a general human condition, not a failure peculiar to him. The scene also shows protection taking a shape indistinguishable from harm for as long as it is happening.

crossReferences.why: States the principle directly: you may hate what is good for you and love what harms you.
Describes God restricting provision for a reason, another case where a loss is a form of care.
Supplies the reason for this act several ayat later, naming the king who was seizing every sound boat.

studies.applyIt: Think of a setback from this year that you have already filed as simply bad. Write the facts of it in three sentences, with no interpretation attached, and stop there. You are not being asked to decide it was secretly good. You are practising the difference between what happened and the account you built on top of it.

studies.title: Do Not Rebuke Me For Forgetting
studies.meaning: The rebuke arrives as a question that is really a reminder: did I not tell you. Moses does not defend the objection he made. He asks two things instead, that he not be held to account for what he forgot, and that his course not be made hard on him. The commentators note the honesty of the first request. He is not arguing that he was right. He is naming the lapse as a lapse and asking for room.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the first of three exchanges that punctuate the narrative, and the only one where Moses asks for leniency rather than proposing his own penalty. The classical commentators read the sequence as a portrait of a sincere man failing at something specific, and observe that it sits in a surah whose other narratives concern people who admit nothing at all.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, literally to take one another to task. The same verb carries the closing prayer of the second surah, where a community asks not to be charged with what it forgets.
To cover a person with something oppressive until it overtakes them. He is not asking to be released from the condition, only that keeping it not be made heavier than he can carry.
The exact opposite of ease, and the word the Quran pairs with ease in its promise that the two travel together. Here it describes the shape a demand can take when it is tightened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Companionship on a journey ran on unwritten rules everyone knew. You did not slow the party, you did not question the route in front of others, and you accepted the leader's terms or left at the next settlement. Asking not to be dismissed for a first offence was a real negotiation with a real outcome. Moses is asking to stay, and asking in the form that would have been recognised as asking.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb Moses uses when he asks not to be held to account is the one that opens the closing prayer of the second surah, where the community asks God not to charge them with what they forget or fall into by mistake. A prophet here uses the language of that prayer, and addresses it to a human companion on a road.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgetting is treated as a real category, distinct from refusal. Moses does not claim his objection was justified and does not pretend the condition was unclear. He names the failure by its actual name and asks for it to be weighed as that. The passage models in conversation what the Quran elsewhere models in prayer: an appeal that does not begin by shrinking what happened.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same request, asking God not to take the community to task for forgetting or error.
Adam is described as forgetting, and the word used is forgetting rather than defiance.
Instructs remembering God whenever you forget, a few ayat before this narrative opens.

studies.applyIt: The next time you get something wrong in front of someone, try naming it exactly. Not an explanation, not a defence of what you meant, and not a larger apology than the thing deserves. Say what you missed and ask for the room you actually need. Most of the difficulty in owning a mistake is in resisting the urge to resize it.

studies.title: A Soul For No Soul
studies.meaning: The second act is worse and the objection is sharper. A boy is met and killed, and Moses protests on a legal intuition anyone would share: a life taken where no life was owed. His verdict escalates from grave to abhorrent. The commentators observe that his phrasing appeals to a principle rather than to feeling, and that the passage records his outrage without correcting it. What gets corrected afterwards is only the fact he was missing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the second of the narrative's three acts. Classical commentators discuss the boy's age on the strength of differing reports and reach no agreement. They are careful to note that the deed is explained within the passage itself as done on an instruction that was not the servant's own, and they read Moses's protest as the response a prophet entrusted with a law would necessarily give.

keyTerms.note: From a root joining cleanness and growth. Early reciters read the word in two forms, one leaning towards innocence of blood guilt and the other towards purity of soul, and the tradition preserves both.
Stronger than the word he used about the boat. Its root supplies the Quran's term for what is disowned and refused, naming something a community would decline to recognise as acceptable at all.
The word covers both a child and a young man not yet grown, which is why the commentators debate his age and settle nothing. The passage itself supplies no number and no description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blood was the most tightly governed thing in Arabian society. A killing outside the rules of retaliation could set tribes against one another for generations, and elaborate machinery existed to stop that: blood money counted in camels, mediators, oaths sworn by fifty men of a clan. Moses's phrase about a soul for no soul is the language of that system. It is the objection a listener in Mecca would have made in the same words.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Moses uses for this deed occurs three times in the Quran, and two of the three are in this surah. The other stands a few ayat later, describing a punishment inside the narrative that follows this one. The same rare adjective is applied once to a human act that shocks a prophet and once to a divine one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moses is never told that his principle was wrong. He is told he lacked a fact. The distinction matters. The passage does not suspend moral judgement in favour of mystery, and it does not offer the servant's act as a model for anybody. It reports an event whose explanation was withheld and then supplied, and it insists both times that the act was not the servant's own decision to make.

crossReferences.why: States the gravity of taking one life where no life was owed, in the terms Moses reaches for here.
Names the prohibition on killing that Moses's protest assumes as settled common ground.
Gives the explanation for this act in the servant's own words, at the end of the narrative.

studies.applyIt: Hold on to the discomfort this scene gives you rather than resolving it quickly. Moses objected, and the Quran preserved the objection. If you have been taught that faith means feeling nothing when something looks wrong, notice today that a prophet said so out loud twice and was answered rather than silenced.

studies.title: Then Do Not Keep Company
studies.meaning: The rebuke returns with one word added, a direct address that makes it personal. Moses does not apologise a second time. He sets his own penalty, and sets it high: one more question and the companionship ends. Then he concedes that sufficient grounds have already been given. The commentators note what he does not do. He asks for no third chance, and instead names the condition under which losing his place would be fair.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's third narrative is carried almost entirely in dialogue, with the acts themselves reported in a clause or two. Classical commentators observe that this exchange is the turning point: after it the story runs to its end without another rebuke, because the next objection Moses raises is the one that closes the journey.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for a companion, in a form meaning to accompany continuously. The verb occurs only here in the Quran, at the moment the companionship is put at risk by the man who asked for it.
The word for a reason offered and accepted. Moses uses it of the other man: you have reached the point of having grounds against me, so the parting would not be unjust.
The same rare word of nearness that described where the servant's knowledge came from, now spoken by Moses of himself. The grounds would come from his own conduct and nowhere else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travelling companionship had a recognised shape. Men agreed to accompany one another to a destination, shared water and night watches, and parting early carried a cost and sometimes a stain. To say do not keep company with me was to invoke a known ending rather than to storm off. Moses is putting the terms of his own dismissal on the record, in front of the person who would carry it out.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb Moses uses for keeping company appears nowhere else in the Quran in this form. The word he chooses for where his grounds would come from is the same rare word of nearness used eleven ayat earlier of the servant's knowledge. Within one narrative it marks a gift given by God and a failing owned by a man.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accountability is shown being taken up rather than imposed. The servant makes no threat; Moses proposes the terms against himself, and the passage lets that stand as the mark of a sincere man. It also shows a limit fixed in advance instead of argued about afterwards, which is why the parting, when it finally comes, arrives without a quarrel between them.

crossReferences.why: Sets the original condition that Moses has now broken twice and is here restating in his own words.
Joseph meets his brothers' admission without recrimination, another scene where an owned fault ends an argument.
Describes the gentleness in dealing with people who fail that the servant keeps through every refusal.

studies.applyIt: The next time you break something you promised, try naming the consequence yourself before anyone else has to. Not a dramatic one, and not a performance of guilt. Something proportionate that you would actually accept. It is a small thing, and it changes the shape of the conversation more than any apology you could offer instead.

studies.title: A Wall About To Fall
studies.meaning: The two reach a town hungry, ask its people for food, and are refused hospitality. Then the servant rebuilds a collapsing wall for the very people who turned them away, and Moses objects a third time. His objection is a different kind from the first two. Not that harm was done, but that payment was not taken. The commentators dwell on the wording, which says the wall wanted to fall, giving an intention to a thing that has none.
