studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The town goes unnamed, and the commentators offer competing identifications drawn from earlier report literature, which they pass on as reports rather than as fact. What the passage itself establishes is the refusal. The classical readings agree it is placed here to sharpen what the servant does next, not to pronounce judgement on the town or its people.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek a thing from someone, and it occurs only here in the Quran. Asking a settlement for food was not begging in that world but a claim on a duty everyone recognised.
Built from the word for a guest, and also unique to this ayah. Hospitality is phrased as something done to a person rather than offered, so refusing it withholds a category, not a meal.
The verb is used of a bird stooping on prey. Applied to masonry it gives the ruin an intention, and the commentators linger on it: the wall is not leaning, it is on its way down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality was the load-bearing virtue of Arabian life, and refusing a traveller food was close to the worst thing a settlement could become known for. Poets ruined reputations with it for a century. A stranger arriving at dusk expected shelter as a matter of course, because everyone was a stranger somewhere eventually. The town in this ayah does the one thing the first audience would have found genuinely shocking.
studies.didYouKnow: Both the verb for asking a town for food and the verb for taking someone in as a guest occur only here in the whole Quran. Neither is unusual Arabic. They are the plain words of the road, and the Quran uses them once, in the scene where the request they name is turned down.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Good is done for people who have just behaved badly, and no lesson is drawn from that at the time. The servant does not lecture the town, does not withhold the repair to make a point, and does not explain himself to his companion. What the passage establishes is that a benefit can be owed to someone by a route that has nothing to do with whether they deserved it, and that the person doing it need not say so.

crossReferences.why: Abraham receives strangers and feeds them before asking anything, the standard this town fails to meet.
Food is given to captive and needy alike with no thanks expected and no return sought.
Explains why the wall was worth repairing, four ayat later and after the two have parted.

studies.applyIt: Do one useful thing this week for someone who has been ungenerous with you, and do not tell them or anyone else. Keep it small enough that you will actually finish it. The test is not the act. It is getting through the day afterwards without finding a way to let them know it happened.

studies.title: This Is The Parting
studies.meaning: The servant announces the separation before he explains anything, so the explanations arrive as a farewell rather than as an argument to be won. The first concerns the boat. It belonged to poor men working the sea, and a king ahead of them was confiscating every sound vessel by force. Damaging it is what kept it. The commentators note his verb: I intended to make it defective, a deliberate spoiling carried out for a protective end.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The three explanations come in the order the acts occurred, each opening with the same particle that marks a new topic. The classical commentators observe that the king is not named, and that reports supplying a name are drawn from earlier traditions outside the Quran. They relay those without treating them as established, and the passage itself gives only the practice.

keyTerms.note: A noun of separation used twice in the Quran. Its other appearance describes the moment a dying person realises what is happening. The word carries finality rather than a temporary leave-taking.
Not translation but what an event finally turns out to be. The Quran uses this word most heavily in the story of Joseph, for the meaning of dreams that only later events disclose.
The word describes those in real hardship who may still hold some property, which is why owning a working boat does not move these men out of the category.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rulers on both coasts requisitioned shipping, and there was no appeal against it. A king outfitting a fleet took whatever floated, and the owners were paid in nothing at all. Fishermen along those shores dealt with it the way people always have, by keeping their boats looking unprofitable. A hull with a visible hole was worth nothing to a passing official and everything to the family that could patch it afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for parting that opens this passage occurs twice in the Quran. The other is in a description of a person's last hour, at the moment he understands that this is the separation. The same noun marks the end of a journey between two men and the end of a life, and both times it arrives without warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Loss is shown working as protection, and the mechanism is ordinary rather than miraculous. The boat is spoiled so that a confiscating official will pass it over. What the passage adds to that familiar idea is timing. The explanation comes only once the relationship is finished, which suggests understanding was never the price of the arrangement. Moses was asked to endure, and the reasons were given to him anyway.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same rare word for parting, there of the moment a dying person knows what is happening.
God restricting what He gives as a form of care, the same logic stated as a general rule.
Uses the same word for interpretation, of events whose meaning only later outcomes make plain.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you own and think about what it would take to keep it safe rather than to keep it perfect. A dented car nobody wants, a plain phone, a modest front door. Not everything worth protecting is protected by being improved. Some of it is protected by being left visibly unremarkable.

studies.title: Better In Purity And Nearer In Mercy
studies.meaning: The second explanation is the hardest, and the passage keeps it short. The boy's parents were believers. The fear was that he would press them into rebellion and denial. The hope was that their Lord would exchange him for one better in purity and closer in mercy. The commentators are careful with the verbs: fearing and wanting are attributed to the servant, and the exchanging is attributed to God. Nothing here is offered as a general rule.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This explanation is given in the first person plural, unlike the one before it and the one after, a shift the classical commentators discuss at length without agreeing on its force. Reports about the boy's later life circulate in the commentary literature and derive from earlier traditions. The sources relay them and generally mark them as reports rather than as part of the passage.

keyTerms.note: A fear that comes from knowing something rather than from nervousness. The Quran uses this root for the awe of those with knowledge, which is why commentators read it as pointing to what was disclosed.
The same verb Moses used when he asked not to be pressed hard over his forgetting. Here it describes a child's conduct closing over his parents until it covers them entirely.
From a root that joins cleanness with increase, and the same root behind the word Moses used for the innocent soul. What is asked for is a child both clean and growing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A son was a household's security. He worked, he defended, he inherited the standing. A son who turned out badly did not merely disappoint his parents. He could break a family's position with a feud, a debt, or a public dishonour that clung to everyone sharing his name. Arabian society had no way of separating a father's reputation from his son's conduct, which is the situation the fear in this ayah assumes.
studies.didYouKnow: The three explanations use three different subjects. The first says I intended, this one says we feared and we wanted, and the last says your Lord wanted. Classical commentators have discussed that progression for centuries, generally reading it as moving the agency further from the servant as the acts become harder to attribute to any human decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something uncomfortable and then refuses to generalise it. A death is presented as care towards two particular believing parents, on the basis of a future only God knew. The servant's closing statement in the next ayah, that he did none of this on his own authority, is what stops the scene becoming a principle. It reports one case whose reasons were supplied, not a rule about anybody else's.

crossReferences.why: Describes children as a trial for their parents, the general condition this particular case sits inside.
States that wealth and children are a test, without saying how any given test will run.
Ends the explanations by attributing the acts to God's will rather than to the servant's.

studies.applyIt: If you are carrying a fear about someone you love, say the fear out loud to God tonight in your own words, without asking for a particular outcome. The servant in this story feared and then handed the matter over. You are allowed to do the first half honestly. The second half is the part you can practise.

studies.title: I Did Not Do It Myself
studies.meaning: The last explanation is the gentlest and the longest. A wall in the town covered a store of treasure belonging to two orphaned boys, their father had been a righteous man, and God intended them to grow up and dig it out themselves. Then the servant removes himself from the account entirely: I did not do this on my own authority. The commentators note that the father's righteousness is mentioned while the boys' is not, and read the protection as reaching forward a generation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This closes the surah's third narrative, and the commentators read it against the other three stories, all of which turn on possessions, time, and what people cannot see. The contents of the store are described in various ways in earlier report literature, and the classical sources pass those descriptions on as traditions while noting that the passage says only that it belonged to the two boys.

keyTerms.note: The age at which a person is held capable of managing what is his. The Quran uses this word elsewhere for the point at which an orphan's property is handed over to him.
From a verb meaning to pack tightly and put away. The same root names hoarded gold that the Quran condemns, so the difference here is not the storing but who it is being stored for.
A root meaning fit for purpose and free of corruption, used of people and of repairs alike. The same root gives the word for setting a thing right, which is what the servant did to the wall.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People buried valuables. There were no banks, houses were mud brick, and a father who died left his children exposed to relatives and neighbours alike. Burying coin or gold beneath a wall and telling one trusted person was ordinary precaution. The Quran returns again and again to what happens to orphans' property, which tells you how often it went missing, and a collapsing wall over a known cache was an invitation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the maturity these boys are waiting to reach is the word the Quran uses elsewhere for the age at which an orphan is handed his own property. It appears in the dual form only here, for these two brothers. The narrative that opened with Moses asking to be taught sound judgement closes on the vocabulary of coming of age.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The final sentence governs everything before it. The servant disclaims authorship of all three acts, which changes retroactively what the reader has been watching. Nothing in the story was a man exercising superior judgement over a prophet. It was a sequence of instructions carried out and then explained, at the parting, by someone who had been given the reasons in advance and told not to share them until the end.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the maturity at which an orphan's property is handed over to him.
Concerns orphans' property and the care owed to it, the exact situation this scene resolves.
Joseph names the outcome of a long ordeal only once the end of it has arrived.

studies.applyIt: Do something today whose result you will not see. Plant something slow, put money aside for a child, write down what you know for whoever comes after you. Then let it go without checking on it. The wall in this story was repaired for two boys who were not there and never learned who did it.

studies.title: If The Ocean Were Ink
studies.meaning: The surah ends by placing three very different things side by side. First a garden described as hospitality, a word for what a host sets out on arrival, with no wish to be moved from it. Then an image of scale: the sea would run dry before the words of the Lord did, and another sea after it. Then a final instruction that reduces everything to two conditions, righteous work and worship with nothing else added underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that answered questions put by opponents to test the message. The classical sources report a specific occasion for the last ayah in some accounts, concerning a man who prayed and also wanted to be seen praying, though the reports differ and several commentators leave it general. The ayah about the sea is reported in connection with a question about how much knowledge had been given.

keyTerms.note: The word for what a host lays out for a guest on arrival, before the real hosting begins. Calling the garden that suggests it is the reception rather than the whole of what is coming.
From a root meaning to extend or supply, the same root as the word for reinforcement used two clauses later. The image and its answer are built from one root, which the translation cannot show.
The word for a person considered as flesh and skin, rather than the word that emphasises the human as a species or a soul. It is the plainest available term, which is the point of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ink was made from soot and gum and kept in small quantities, and writing was a specialist trade. A scribe measured his supply carefully, and running out mid-document was a real interruption. Setting the sea against an inkwell was not a poetic flourish to people who had watched one being refilled. The comparison worked because everyone knew how little ink a person actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with praise for a Book with no crookedness and closes by saying the words of the Lord would outlast the sea as ink. Its first and last movements are both about the extent of revelation. The word used for the garden here appears only twice in the Quran, and this is one of the two places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The last ayah does two things at once. It denies the messenger any status beyond being human and receiving revelation, which removes him as an object of devotion in the same breath as it establishes his role. And it states the whole requirement in one sentence: do good work, and put nothing beside God in the worship of God. Everything the surah has narrated, the cave, the gardens, the journey, resolves into that.

crossReferences.why: Multiplies the same image: all the trees as pens and seven seas as ink.
The other place the same word for the garden appears, promised to the heirs.
Another place the messenger is told to say he is only a human being.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you did this week for a good reason and ask what the second reason was. There usually is one, and it is usually about how it looked. Do not scold yourself. Just find the next occasion to do the same thing where nobody will know, and see whether you still want to. That is the test this ayah sets.
